requirements.nl_text: Request Number - 328 | Request Title - Feature request: Sending dummy short messages | Request Description - TextSecure could mask meaningful communication between people by occasionally sending dummy random messages to random recipients at random times:  Recipients would be chosen randomly between contacts that knowingly use TextSecure, so it could be recognized as such after decryption and automatically discarded by recipient. "Randomness" should be tweaked to level-out the legitimate messages, spoiling the traffic analysis of traffic retention data, preventing to weigh connections in the deducted social network graph or guessing sleeping/activity patterns. People often have many unused messages in their monthly quota, so those could easily be used with no extra cost, or they value their privacy more than some money. Sender would need to enable this feature (opt-in) and define desired quantity (eg max 100 dummy messages per month, 2 dummy messages for every legitimate one, max 500 messages total counting legitimate and dummy ones...). The feature would need to be aware of roaming (disabled by default, optionally enable) and battery level (do not send if bellow eg. 30%). http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_analysis#Countermeasures Possible extensions:  Recipients could be able to let their peers know, that they do not want to participate in this and do not want to receive messages for whatever reason (opt-out). Recipients could also be chosen randomly between other contacts (those not using TextSecure yet) to promote its use (default message) or a custom explanation by sender. verdict.text:
One caveat first. The study context says non-atomic requirements were excluded, but this is a blind run: 50 source requirements expand to 77 gold units, and 15 have more than one gold unit (328-Signal has 5, 802-Signal has 6). Either the wrong dataset was attached or the exclusion note does not apply here. The results should be read as a mixed set until that is resolved.

Track 1 has real support for only two slots: scope (76 missing) and condition (35 missing). Actor, modalVerb and action have 1, 1 and 4 missing cases, which is too few to say anything about them. On face value, the scope flag rate of 0.18 and condition flag rate of 0.31 look like heavy fabrication. The examples suggest much of this is a scoring artifact instead. In 2943-Signal, 802-Signal#5 and #6, the model simply left out the scope and condition clauses ("<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB> provide …"), and the parser recorded the absent clauses as "filled." Some fabrication is real. 2055-Signal invents the scope "For each incoming message," which also inverts the request, since the request is about outgoing messages. 1504-Signal lifts a scope from the title of what is a non-request. The true fabrication rate is unknown until omission and filling are scored separately.

The model's actual error runs in the opposite direction on actor and modalVerb. It emits <MISSING_ACTOR> and <MISSING_MODAL_VERB> where the gold treats "the App must" as implied: 35 of 71 implied actors and 45 of 76 implied modal verbs. This one behaviour produces 48 of the 51 requirement-level disagreements. The model is over-literal about who acts and how strongly, and inconsistent about it across units of the same request (1692-Signal#1 versus #2).

Conversion similarity reaches roughly 78% of the human ceiling on sequence ratio (0.56 against 0.72) and 71% on Jaccard (0.39 against 0.55). That is a real but moderate gap, and part of it is mechanical. The humans always write <MISSING_SCOPE> and <MISSING_CONDITION>, while the model drops them, and unit misalignment depresses scores further. 802-Signal#5 and #6 pair the model's import with the humans' export, and 222-Signal#1 scores 0 because no unit was matched. The cosine figure (n=3, all zero) is broken and should be ignored.

Paska mostly echoes the placeholder issue. Outputs the model marked complete pass at 81%, while those with placeholders pass at 8%. The dominant smells, "Not requirement" and "Incomplete requirement," are what Paska reports when a sentence contains placeholder tokens instead of a system response. The genuine linguistic smells are few:
- condition placed after the response (6459-Signal, 6424-Signal)
- an OR-coordinated condition (5751-Signal#2)
- an imprecise verb (7310-Signal)

Unit detection under blind prompting over-splits badly. Recall is perfect, but 14 of 35 atomic requests were split, typically into 3 units (2055-Signal into 5). Requests that really are non-atomic were also inflated (328-Signal returned 19 units against 5). Only 27 of 50 unit counts were exact.

The most useful next step is to fix the measurement before comparing strategies. The parser should treat an absent clause as omitted, not filled, or the prompt should require explicit scope and condition placeholders. The prompt should also state that a generic "the App must" counts as implied and should be filled. After that, rerun this condition. With 50 requirements, and fewer than five missing cases for three of the slots, this run identifies failure modes but cannot rank zsl against fsl or cot.
